title: This too trains
hook: how to bear a fever: this too is exercise (Discourses 3.10)

segments.voice: Yesterday: found doing this, what you'd be glad to be doing when the end comes. Your line was attending to nothing but my own will. What did you do on purpose? Day four hundred nineteen.
screen: `FOUND DOING THIS — ATTENDING TO NOTHING BUT MY OWN WILL.`

segments.voice: The thermometer beeps, and the week's plans quietly fall apart. Meetings get canceled, the to-do list sits there, and on top of feeling awful it's easy to feel useless, as if life has been put on pause until you're well again. Epictetus knew something about bodies that don't cooperate. Ancient writers say he was lame. So when he talks about illness, he isn't speaking from a healthy distance. Today: nosos.
screen: `THE THERMOMETER BEEPS.` → `LIFE ON PAUSE.` → `ANCIENT WRITERS SAY HE WAS LAME.`

segments.voice: This is Discourses book three, chapter ten: how we should bear illness. Epictetus starts with advice that sounds almost like a packing list. Keep your principles ready for each situation: at the table, the ones about eating; in the bath, the ones about bathing; in bed, the ones about lying in bed. And then, the ones about fever. Because a fever, he says, is also part of life, like walking, or sailing, or traveling. It isn't a pause. It's a different kind of practice. So what does it mean to bear a fever well? He's specific. Not blaming God or other people. Not being crushed by what's happening. Doing what needs to be done. When the doctor comes in, not dreading what he'll say, and not being giddy if he says you're doing well. In other words, the same things he asks of you on a healthy day, just in a smaller room. This too is training, he says. A sick day isn't a day off from becoming who you want to be. In some ways it's a clear day for it, because the usual props are gone. You can't prove anything by being busy. You can only be patient, honest about how you feel, and kind to whoever brings you the soup. This isn't a reason to ignore medicine or push through when your body needs rest. Resting well is the practice. Epictetus' point is that the person lying there is still training, and still free.
screen: `PRINCIPLES READY FOR EVERY ROOM.` · `A FEVER IS PART OF LIFE TOO.` · `NOT BLAMING, NOT CRUSHED.` · `REST WELL: THAT'S THE PRACTICE.` · then, large: `THIS TOO TRAINS.`

segments.voice: Sit or lie down, whichever is kinder to your body right now. Breathe. Scan gently from head to feet. Notice any ache, tiredness, tightness or illness, big or small. Don't fight it and don't dramatize it. Say to yourself, plainly: this is here. Then ask: how would I like to carry this today? Maybe with patience, maybe with honesty, maybe by simply resting well. Let the breath do the rest. The bell holds the time.
Nosos. Greek for sickness: Epictetus on illness, a fever is part of life, and bearing it well, without blame or despair, is practice like any other.
Your line: resting well is the practice. If you're unwell today, or tired, or sore, rest well, and treat even that as practice. Day four hundred nineteen.

howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners who are ill treat recovery as part of their practice: following medical care, resting, and working on patience rather than blame.

original.note: Greek nosos: sickness, disease; Discourses 3.10 is on how to bear it.

trapdoor: what you thought: be tough and ignore being sick.
what it means: rest, follow care, and bear illness without blame or despair; that's training too.
what a scholar hears: later sources (Origen, quoting Celsus; Simplicius) say Epictetus was lame, and they disagree on whether it came from mistreatment or illness.
recall: the senator who kept going in

sources.ref: Origen, Against Celsus 7.53; Simplicius, Commentary on the Enchiridion

notes: Discourses 3.10 paraphrased: principles ready at hand (dinner, bath, bed); fever as part of life; bearing fever well (not blaming God or man, not afflicted, the physician's visit); 'this too is a kind of exercise/test'. Confirm details.
Epictetus' lameness: Origen (Contra Celsum 7.53) reports the story of his master twisting his leg; Simplicius says he was lame from childhood; the Suda says from rheumatism. Confirm the summary.
The script adds that this isn't a reason to ignore medicine; check framing.

Editor review (2026-10-01): hook no longer opens on a sickbed (days 412 and 418 already use the bed/sick-student image) and no longer tells the listener they feel useless; 'walked with a limp for much of his life' cut to 'ancient writers say he was lame' (the sources disagree on when and why); removed 'not clinging, not despairing', which aren't in 3.10's list; softened the superlative 'one of the best days'.
